newsitem.title: CENTRAL AFRICAN REPUBLIC: Troops revolt again in Central African Republic.
newsitem.headline: Troops revolt again in Central African Republic.

text.p: Dissidents in the Central African Republic's army mutinied for a third time this year on Saturday and French troops patrolled the streets of the capital to protect key points, military sources said.

President Ange-Felix Patasse, speaking in Rome where he is attending the World Food Summit, dismissed the revolt as the work of common criminals. "It is not a mutiny. Some common law prisoners have escaped and are trying to create panic. That is all," he said.

Troops from former colonial power France, who put down a revolt that threatened to topple Patasse in May, were patrolling the deserted city centre with members of the loyalist presidential guard, witnesses said.
"French soldiers have been deployed in Bangui to assure the safety of certain sensitive areas," a French official said in Paris.

Scattered firing could be heard in the city early in the day but the precise whereabouts of the dissidents remained unclear. There were no immediate reports of looting that accompanied the May mutiny and a pay revolt in April.

Radio France International, quoting one of the dissidents and sources close to Prime Minister Jean-Paul Ngoumpande, said the revolt began at Kassai barracks outside the city. The dissident said they would stay in the barracks at present.
A soldier contacted by telephone by Reuters in Kassai barracks said earlier about 200 soldiers had gone to various districts to try to disarm militia loyal to Patasse.
Army sources linked the latest revolt to a bid on Friday to arrest a nephew of former military leader Andre Kolingba, whom Patasse defeated in a 1993 presidential poll.
The nephew, an army captain, was out on parole after serving a jail sentence for embezzlement and other charges, they added.
Earlier army sources said dissidents were moving from the eastern districts towards the presidential palace, the radio and television station and Patasse's residential villa.
"They broke into the armoury around midnight and stole arms and then firing broke out," a senior loyalist officer said.

Sources close to the dissidents said they had revived demands for wages from 1992 and 1993 and that Patasse revoked a decree ordering the Regiment for the Operational Defence of the Territory (RDOT) to Bouar, 80 km (50 miles) from Bangui. The regiment was heaviliy involved in the earlier revolts.

France has an important military base in Central African Republic, one of the world's poorest countries, under defence accords between Paris and its former African colonies. Patasse, a civilian, invoked those accords in May to secure French help against the mutineers.

The Central African Republic base has been key in France's long history of military intervention in Africa, including in Rwanda where Paris is again preparing to send troops in a multinational mission to help war refugees.
A national conference after the May revolt agreed on a number of reforms to improve the lot of soldiers by creating a professional army with a fuller role in the life of the nation.

But lingering friction remains. The army is dominated by members of former self-styled emperor Jean-Bedel Bokassa's Gbaka tribe but Kolingba's Yakoma tribe is well-represented. Bokassa, ousted in 1979 and later disgraced, died on November 3 aged 75.
